newsitem.title: USA: Coffee trade expects price gains to continue.
newsitem.headline: Coffee trade expects price gains to continue.

text.p: Coffee prices have surged more than 50 percent since the start of the year, and U.S. industry members meeting at the National Coffee Association convention this week say prices are likely to rise further because supplies remain tight.

Low inventory levels in consuming and producing countries, combined with the prospect of smaller crops in many Latin American countries and the Association of Coffee Producing Countries' (ACPC) cut in export quotas for the first half of 1997, have helped pushed prices to two-year highs in New York.

"The sentiment here is so bullish," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "It appears to be mostly one-sided. People are not saying where do you think the market is going, but how high is it going."
Many delegates attending the convention said prices should have little problem breaching 200.00 cents ($2) per pound in the coming weeks.
On Friday, the nearby March contract on the New York Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange jumped 7.30 cents, to 190.40 cents, while most-active May soared 5.75 cents, to 176.85 cents.

The price surge on Friday came despite a bearish 1997/98 Brazil crop forecast. Leon Yallouz, a former U.S. Department of Agriculture representative, pegged the coming Brazil harvest at 27.5 million 60-kg bags. Preliminary estimates out of Brazil have generally ranged between 18 million and 23 million bags.
"Even those who want to be bearish say it is hard when there is no physical coffee," Ganes said.
Stocks at roasting plants have dwindled the past few months during the peak season for demand, but some industry sources cautioned that roastings typically slow down in the spring.
Additionally, the great desparity between arabica futures and cheaper robusta futures traded in London could prompt some roasters to juggle their blends.

But as winter season approaches in the Southern Hemisphere, industry members say any threat of frost in top-grower Brazil is likely to heighten supply jitters -- and continue to bolster the futures market.
